17.1                    Objectives

To:

  • Protect the Company’s business information - operation assets and any customer or partner information within its custody by safeguarding its confidentiality, integrity and availability.
  • Establish responsibility and accountability for cybersecurity within the Company and the ship.
  • Encourage Management and staff to maintain an appropriate level of awareness, knowledge and skill, allowing them to minimize the occurrence and severity of cybersecurity incidents.
  • Ensure that the ship can continue its commercial and service activities in the event of cybersecurity incidents.

17.2                    Purpose

To:

  • Identify the personnel, data, devices, IT/OT and communication systems that pose risks to ship operations when disrupted and define personnel roles and responsibilities for cyber risk management.
  • Protect against cybersecurity events by implementing risk control processes, measures and contingency planning.
  • Detect cybersecurity events promptly by developing and implementing appropriate measurements.
  • Respond to cyber events with procedures and plans to restore the impaired systems necessary for shipping operations or services.
  • Recover after cybersecurity events with the correct measures to backup and restore impacted cyber systems necessary for shipping operations.

Cybersecurity Framework

17.3                    Cyber Risk Management

The Company assesses the risks arising from Information Technology (IT) and Operation Technology (OT) use and establishes appropriate safeguards against cyber incidents.

The Cybersecurity Risk Management includes:

  • Identification of the systems, assets, data, and capabilities, which, if disrupted, can threaten the Company or ship’s operations and safety
  • Identification of the relevant threats and vulnerabilities, assessment of risk exposure, and development of protection measures
  • Identification of the roles and responsibilities of users ashore and onboard
  • Protective measures against cyber incidents ensuring operations continuity. These include, among others:
    • Network configuration
    • Network and system access control
    • Communication and boundary defense
    • Protection and detection software.
  • Activities and measures to prepare, respond and provide resilience against cyber incidents. These include, among others:
    • Training and awareness
    • Software maintenance
    • Remote and local access
    • Access privileges
    • Measures for removable media use
    • Proper equipment disposal.

17.4                    Governance

17.4.1            Top Management Leadership and Commitment

The Company demonstrates its commitment to cybersecurity, which extends to senior levels of the organization through the provision of appropriate resources to develop and maintain associated controls.

The Top Management:

  • Enforces behaviors mandated by the cybersecurity policy.
  • Monitors the employees' familiarization and awareness of potential cyber threats.
  • Trains employees on strategies preventing or responding to cyber threats.
  • Guides employees towards understanding and adhering to the best cybersecurity practices relevant to their job responsibilities.
  • Sets appropriate procedures for reporting and investigation of all cyber-related incidents.
  • Monitors and systematically reviews the performance and effectiveness of the cybersecurity policy and procedures.
  • Continually improves the organization’s cybersecurity resilience based on objective measurements.

17.4.2            Cybersecurity Policy

The Company’s Top Management treats cybersecurity management issues with the same responsibility and importance as the entire business operations.

In Chapter 2 - APPENDIX IX, the cybersecurity policy guarantees the safety and security of Company’s personnel and assets.

17.4.3            Roles, Responsibilities and Authorities

Cybersecurity Company Officer (CySCO):

  • Design, implement and communicate the cybersecurity policy and procedures to all relevant interested parties.
  • Maintain an IT/OT asset inventory and manage the risks associated to them.
  • Manage user profiles & passwords in the ship network.
  • Ensure that all cybersecurity procedures are in place and documented.
  • Establish and maintain improvement plans and targets and report achievements.
  • Approve expenditure on cybersecurity-related matters, in cooperation with the GM.
  • Audit and review the cybersecurity policy and procedures.
  • Declare and investigate cybersecurity incidents.
  • Participate in Emergency Response Team.
  • Attend Management Review Meetings.

The Cybersecurity Company Officer is the IT Coordinator.

IT Department is responsible to:

Communicate to all employees and monitor the proper implementation of this manual.

Master:

  • Ensure that all personnel onboard implement the required procedures according to their responsibilities regarding the cybersecurity policy.
  • Ensure that all personnel onboard observe and maintain communications' confidentiality as required by the Company and applicable regulations.
  • Declare cybersecurity incidents.
  • Review the operation of cybersecurity controls within ship areas.
  • Request well defined necessary information security equipment and solutions.

Cybersecurity Ship Officer (CySSO):

  • Ensure that cybersecurity controls onboard are in place and documented.
  • Identify and manage cybersecurity incidents onboard.
  • Take action to prevent a cybersecurity incident from occurring or escalating, if possible.
  • Support the IT Department for troubleshooting cyber related incidents.
  • Maintain an IT/OT asset inventory onboard in cooperation with the IT Department.

The Cybersecurity Ship Officer is the MASTER

Company ERT members: Respond as required to a cyber incident and implement all necessary actions.

All Company personnel: Implement the required procedures according to your responsibilities.

17.4.4            Regulatory and Legislative Requirements

This Cybersecurity Manual complies with:

  • IMO Resolution MSC.428(98) & MSC-FAL.1/Circ.3 5 July 2017
  • The Guidelines on Cyber Security Onboard Ships - BIMCO version 1, 2, 3, 4,

and is in line with the relevant clauses of the following International Standards:

  • ISO/IEC 27001:2013
  • ISA 62443-2-1:2009
  • ISA 62443-3-3:2013
  • IEC 61162-460
  • NIST.SP.800-53.

17.4.5            Sources of Cybersecurity Information

The Company keeps constant contact with authorities and special interest groups in order to maintain an updated cybersecurity information database. These sources for cybersecurity information could be:

  • Flag States
  • Classification Societies
  • Industry bodies such as OCIMF, BIMCO, INTERTANKO, ICS
  • National and International Cybersecurity Organizations (e.g.  NIST-SPs, ISO 27032)
  • Specialist Cyber External Consultants
  • Cybersecurity Media and Forums.

17.4.6            Corporate Mobile Device Policy

The purpose of this policy is to set out the controls that must be in place when using mobile devices and to mitigate the following risks:

  • Loss or theft of mobile devices, including the data on them
  • Compromise of classified information through observation by the public
  • Introduction of viruses and malware to the network
  • Loss of reputation.

Corporate mobile devices include items such as:

  • Laptops
  • Notebooks
  • Tablet devices
  • Smartphones.

The Company, through the IT Department, provides support for problem resolution and maintenance.

Employees ashore & onboard:

  • When possible, ensure the device is transported in a protective case.
  • DO NOT leave the device unattended in public view.
  • DO NOT remove any identifying marks on the device such as a company asset tag or serial number.
  • Ensure the device is locked when being stored and the key is not easily accessible.
  • DO NOT add peripheral hardware to the device without the approval of the IT Department.
  • You can hold classified information on the device only when authorized and appropriate controls (e.g., encryption) are in place.
  • DO NOT keep personal identification information within the device.
  • Ensure the device screen locks after a short period of not being used and an access code or password is needed to unlock it.
  • DO NOT use the device for personal activities.
  • You MUST NOT install any unauthorized software or change the configuration or setup of the device.
  • Where possible, the device will use data encryption.
  • Where applicable, virus protection secures the device.
  • DO NOT disable virus protection on the device.
  • DO NOT connect the device to non-corporate networks such as wireless or the Internet unless a secure VPN is used.

17.4.7            Bring Your Own Device Policy

The purpose of this policy is to set out the controls that must be in place when using personal mobile devices. Personal mobile devices include items such as:

  • Laptops
  • Notebooks
  • Tablet devices
  • Smartphones
  • Smartwatches.

Onboard

  • All personal owned mobile devices must have a password-protected screensaver.
  • It is prohibited to connect your personal mobile devices to the ship’s Business network, IT/OT and Communication systems.
  • DO NOT store corporate data on personal devices.
  • It is prohibited to connect corporate USB flash disks to personal mobile devices.
  • Rooted (Android), jailbroken (iOS) or unlocked mobile devices CANNOT be used.
  • Use Antivirus and Internet security software to protect your personal mobile device.
  • It is prohibited to charge your mobile devices in unauthorized stations.

Ashore

  • It is prohibited to:
  • Connect corporate USB flash disks to personal mobile devices.
  • Store corporate data on personal devices.
  • Use Rooted (Android), jailbroken (iOS) or unlocked mobile devices.
  • All personal owned mobile devices must have a password-protected screensaver.

17.5                    Supply Chain Management

17.5.1            Supplier Relationships

Information security requirements vary according to the type of contractual relationship that exists with each supplier and the goods or services delivered.

The Company in general will apply the following:

  • The information security requirements and controls are formally documented in a contractual agreement.
  • Separate Non-Disclosure Agreements where a more specific level of control over confidentiality is required.
  • Appropriate due diligence in the selection and approval of new suppliers.
  • The information security provisions for existing suppliers are clearly defined.
  • Remote access by suppliers is implemented via approved methods that comply with the Company’s information security policies.
  • Basic information security principles such as least privilege, separation of duties and defense in depth.
  • The supplier is expected to exercise adequate control over the cybersecurity policies and procedures used within sub-contractors who play a part in the supply chain of delivery of goods or services to the Company.
  • Awareness training is carried out by both parties to the agreement.

The selection of required controls is based upon a comprehensive RA taking into account information security requirements, the product or service to be supplied, its criticality to the Company and the capabilities of the supplier.

For the control of security risks, the company examines very carefully and accordingly adjusts:

  • The facilities in which external associates or customers have access to
  • The access kind that is given (physical, networked, logical, remote or local)
  • The works – procedures, the action log requirements and the assignment contracts
  • The protection of the company’s interest.
  • The protection and handling requirements of any confidential and/or personal data transferred to external associates.

17.5.2            Due Diligence

The Company, before contracting with a contractor/supplier, exercises due diligence in reaching as full an understanding as possible of his information security approach and controls.

17.5.3            Addressing Security Within Supplier Agreements

Once a potential supplier has been positively assessed with due diligence, the information security requirements of the Company are reflected within the written contractual agreement.

This agreement takes into account the classification of any information (if used by the Company) that is to be processed by the supplier, legal and regulatory requirements and any additional information security controls required.

17.5.4            Managing Changes to Supplier Services

Changes to services provided by suppliers are subject to the Company’s MoC procedure. This process includes the requirement to assess any information security implications of changes so that the effectiveness of controls is maintained.

17.6                    Identify Threats

All IT and OT systems are subject to misuse and are vulnerable to attacks. Attackers can use vulnerabilities to access computers or network-related resources having a "potential for unintended use". A vulnerability is not an attack but an exploitable weak point.

Cyber threats can lead to potential security violations (malicious or otherwise). They exist because of system weaknesses.

Cyber threats for IT/OT & Communication systems are common both onboard and ashore.

 

The table below includes the most usual threat actors, along with the types of groups capable of committing them:

 

Group

Motivation

Objective

Activists (including disgruntled employees)

 

  • Reputational damage
  • Operations disruption
  • Data destruction
  • Publication of sensitive data
  • Media attention

Criminals

  • Financial gain
  • Espionage
  • Selling stolen data
  • Ransoming stolen data
  • Ransoming system operability
  • Arranging fraudulent cargo transportation

Opportunists

  • Challenge/Fun/Skill show-off
  • Financial gain

Getting through cybersecurity defenses

  • States
  • State-sponsored organizations
  • Terrorists
  • Political/Financial gain
  • Espionage
  • Gaining knowledge
  • Disruption to economies and critical national infrastructure

Accidental actors

No malicious motive but still end up causing unintended harm through bad luck, lack of knowledge, or lack of care

-

 

A cyberattack is where an attacker tries to gain unauthorized access to an IT/OT and communication system for the purpose of theft, extortion, disruption or other nefarious reasons. Of course, a large number of security incidents are caused by insiders – whether through negligence or malice. 

A ship shore drill involving cyber security incidents including phishing or penetration test should be done on an annual basis with each one of the Company’s Managed vessel

17.6.1            Cyber Attack Types

17.6.1.1         Phishing & Social Engineering Attacks

Phishing involves sending emails that appear to be from trusted sources. The aim is to gain your sensitive information, or to spread malware. Part confidence trick and part hacking, phishing is one of the easiest (and therefore, the most common) ways to breach a Company’s security. Think of it as a way to find out your password – a highly effective password attack.

Spear phishing  uses a more focused approach. These attacks require a bit more research on an individual or a target user group. For example, with a little online research, a phisher can identify your colleague’s email addresses and send what appears to be a legitimate email from a trusted source instructing your users to download a file (malware), or even hand over the login details to a key business application.

          Train the users on the correct protocols for password security.

          Hover the mouse over URL link to check the legitimacy of the web site.

          Look at email header “Reply-to” and “Return-Path” to ensure it matches the source you believe the email is from.

17.6.1.2         Password Attacks & Credential Reuse

Despite the risks being well known, people fail to use strong passwords, inadvertently give them away to phishing scammers or scribble them on bits of paper.

A hacker will use an array of password hacking techniques, from using lists of common ‘weak’ passwords, to sophisticated ‘Rainbow table’ attacks, using previously hacked/cracked lists of hashed passwords.

          Educate your users on phishing methods.

          Encourage & enforce the use of strong, unique passwords.

          Implement an account lockout policy.

          Prohibit the use of default passwords.

17.6.1.3         Malware attack

Malicious software can be described as unwanted software that is installed in a system without the user’s consent. It can attach itself to legitimate code and propagate. It can lurk in useful applications or replicate itself across the Internet.

17.6.1.4         Denial-of-Service Attacks

There’s a variety of DoS and DDoS (Distributed Denial of Service) attacks which can have devastating consequences. The most common are teardrop attack, smurf attack, TCP SYN flood attack, ping-of-death, and botnets.

DoS & DDoS attacks hurt businesses by flooding target web servers with requests – stopping regular users connecting. This means website downtime, disappointed customers, reputation damage and can even result in data losses & compensation payouts.

          If you don’t have “always-on” DoS protection, minimise the impact.

          It is not enough to hope that your firewalls and ISP are able to stop the heavy loads that attackers use today. There are 3 main options to consider for DoS protection:

o         On-premise protection to identify, filter, detect and protect your network.

o         Cloud-based counteraction to deflect, absorb, reroute and scrub.

o         Hybrid solution (combining on-prem and cloud DoS protection).

17.6.1.5         Man-in-the-Middle (MitM)

A MitM attack is when a hacker inserts themselves between two legitimate hosts. It’s the cyber equivalent of eavesdropping on a private conversation. In fact, an eavesdropping attack is a common type of attack itself. But the MitM attack goes a step further since it has the added malevolence of disguising itself as one, or both of the people speaking.

This means it doesn’t just intercept and listen into messages between clients and servers. It can also change the messages and plant requests that appear to be from a legitimate source. These types of attacks are notoriously difficult to detect – but there are preventative measures.

          Use SSL certificates (HTTPS, not just HTTP) to enhance security (and user trust) in Company’s website/extranet.

          Consider an Intrusion Detection System (IDS).

          Set-up a VPN to add additional layers of protection over Wi-Fi (and other confidential networks).

17.6.1.6         Structured Query Language (SQL) Injections

An SQL injection is when malicious code is inserted into an SQL database. For an attacker, it can be as simple as submitting malicious code into a website’s search box.

Once the code’s been unleashed, it can read, modify or delete the data. Some SQL attacks can even shutdown a database and issue commands to the operating system.

          Apply a least-privilege permissions model in the databases.

          Stick to stored procedures (exclude dynamic SQL) and prepared statements (parameterized queries).

          Validate SQL data inputs against a whitelist.

17.6.1.7         Zero-day Exploit

If a user uncovers a security risk in a program, they may well notify the software company so they can develop and issue a security patch to fix the issue.

This well-meaning user has just exposed a vulnerability to the world. While the software developers rush to fix the problem, hackers get busy exploiting it.

Zero-day attacks are usually the most difficult to defend against, since the precise nature of the attack is only available after it has happened.

          Keep operating systems and application software up to date.

          Use virtual LANS to protect transmitted data by making use of a firewall.

          Protect against wireless malware attacks with a secure Wi-Fi system.

          Stick to websites with SSL certificates.

          DO NOT use cracked/unknown applications.

17.6.1.8         Cross-site Scripting (XSS)

This attack usually runs in conjunction with social engineering because it requires a user to visit a web page where the hacker has inserted malicious script.

When you land on an infected web page, the malicious payload can leave you exposed to a variety of unpleasant consequences. In a worst-case scenario, the XSS attack can access webcams, microphones, log keystrokes and even take remote control over the user’s machine. The most common vehicle is JavaScript as it is so widely used across the web.

          Ensure users are educated on phishing techniques.

          Sanitize the data input by users with an HTTP request.

          Run XXS vulnerability tests.

17.6.1.9         Drive-by-downloads

A drive-by download attack can take advantage of an operating system, web browser or app that has vulnerabilities (due to a lack of security updates). It can be transmitted when the user simply views an email, pop-up or website.

          Keep your OS and browsers updated.

          Stick to trusted sites you would normally use.

          Keep only apps and programs you need – the more plug-ins, the more weak spots you may have.

17.6.2            Cyber-attack Stages

Cyberattacks occur in 4 stages:

  1. Survey / Reconnaissance: Attackers use:
    • Open/public sources to gain information about the Company, ships, or seafarer to prepare for a cyber attack.
    • Social media, technical forums, and hidden properties in websites, documents, and publications to identify technical, procedural, and physical vulnerabilities.
  2. Delivery: Attackers may attempt to access Company and ship systems and data remotely or directly from within the Company or ships. Examples of the methods used include:
    • Company online services, including cargo or consignment tracking systems
    • Sending emails containing malicious files or links to malicious websites to personnel
    • Providing infected removable media, for example, as part of a software update for an onboard system
    • Creating false or misleading websites encouraging the personnel's disclosure of user account information.
  3. Breach: The extent to which an attacker can breach a Company or ship system depends on the vulnerability the attacker finds and the attack method he employs. Depending on the breach significance, an attacker may be able to:
    • Make changes that affect the system's operation.
    • Gain access to sensitive data, e.g., cargo manifests or crew/passenger lists.
    • Gain complete control over a system, e.g., main engine.

A breach might not result in any apparent changes to the equipment status.

 

  1. Effect: The attacker's motivation and objectives determine the impact his actions have on the Company or ship system and data. An attacker may explore systems, expand access and/or make sure that he can return to the system to:
    • Cause complete denial of service on business systems.
    • Enable other forms of crime, for example, piracy, theft, and fraud.
    • Manipulate crew or passenger/visitor lists, cargo manifests, stow plans, etc. This manipulation subsequently allows the fraudulent transport of illegal cargo or may facilitate thefts.
    • Disrupt normal operation of the Company's and ship's systems, for example, by deleting critical information or overloading the Company's systems.
    • Install permanent tools or a key logger to keep and maintain access to the system.
    • Execute new attacks.

The users of IT and OT systems onboard and ashore must:

          Know the cybersecurity threats.

          Receive training to identify and mitigate such risks.

17.7                    Identify Vulnerabilities

The Company:

  • Adopts a risk management approach to assess and mitigate the risks associated with the threat actors relevant to its activities.
  • Prioritizes cybersecurity risks.
  • Assesses potential threats.
  • Assesses the systems and procedures onboard and ashore to map the robustness to handle the current threat level.
  • Decides on appropriate and proportionate investment in a security controls portfolio to mitigate risks with the most significant potential impact.

These vulnerability assessments, resulting in a strategy centered around the key risks, involve:

  • Identification and evaluation of essential or sensitive assets and infrastructure considered essential to protect as well as the external infrastructure systems on which they depend.
  • Identification of the ship's business processes using the assets and infrastructure to assess the criticality of assets and understand any internal/external dependencies.
  • Identification and assessment of risks arising from possible threats to assets and infrastructure, vulnerabilities, and the likelihood of their occurrence, to establish the need for and to prioritize security measures.
  • Identification, assessment, selection, and prioritization of security controls and procedural changes, based on their costs, the level of effectiveness in reducing the risk, and any impact on the ship's operations.
  • Identification of the overall residual risk acceptability, including human factors and weaknesses in the infrastructure, policies, and procedures, based on the selected security controls.

17.7.1            Determination of Vulnerability Onboard

General RA guidance:

          Standalone systems are less vulnerable to cyberattacks than systems attached to uncontrolled networks or directly to the internet.

          Understand how critical shipboard systems might connect to uncontrolled networks.

          Consider the human element since personnel actions initiate many incidents.

 

Onboard systems include:

  • Bridge systems
  • Cargo handling and Management Systems
  • Communication systems
  • Access control systems
  • Propulsion and machinery management and power control systems
  • Administrative and crew welfare systems.

Digital communication helps conduct business, manage operations and stay in touch with the Office. Furthermore, critical ship systems essential for the safety of navigation, power, and cargo management are extensively digitalized and connected to the Internet for a wide variety of functions.

Consider the risks of misunderstood, unknown, and uncoordinated remote access to an operating ship as a critical part of the RA.

The following are common cyber vulnerabilities:

  • Obsolete and unsupported operating systems
  • Outdated or missing antivirus software and malware protection
  • Inadequate security configurations
  • The use of default administrator accounts and passwords
  • Ineffective network management not based on the least privilege principle
  • Shipboard computer networks lacking boundary protection measures and network segmentation
  • Safety-critical equipment or systems permanently connected to the shore side
  • Inadequately trained and/or skilled staff to manage cyber risks
  • Missing, inadequate, or untested contingency plans and procedures
  • Inadequate access controls for third parties, including contractors and service providers.

Consider the following:

  • The maker's and service provider's cybersecurity awareness and procedures
  • The maturity of their cybersecurity awareness and procedures.

Shoreside and onboard personnel may be unaware of how some equipment providers maintain remote access to equipment and its network system.

 

The Company shall:

          Ask these companies for a cybersecurity policy, including training and governance procedures for the accessible IT and OT systems onboard.

          Challenge the internal cyber network security governance.

          Get a cybersecurity assurance when considering future contracts and services.

17.7.2            Determination of Vulnerability Ashore

IT Department:

  • Assess the exposure risk and extent of ICT systems exposure to cyberattacks.
  • Consider the ICT infrastructure at the Office, including Server Room and desk workstations vulnerable to cyberattacks. These systems' cybersecurity follows the same principles as the onboard systems.
  • Consider the network's physical layout and vital network devices' physical location, including servers, switches, firewalls, and cabling. This helps restrict access and maintain the physical security of the network installation and control network entry points.
  • Run periodic system vulnerability scans, seeking gaps in protective coverage and system configuration.
  • Identify and evaluate each system's connections with reported vulnerabilities to determine those vulnerabilities' criticality and prioritize patching those systems accordingly.
  • Use a process feeding recognized and discovered vulnerabilities from scans and asset assessments back to the RA process for prioritization and mitigation actions.

Important ICT systems are:

  • Servers
  • Workstations/thin-clients
  • Network equipment (switches, routers, firewalls)
  • Printers/scanners
  • Mobile devices (smartphones, tablets).

Any network design must include infrastructure for administering and managing the network. This may include installing network management software on dedicated workstations and servers providing file sharing, email, and other services to the network.

17.8                    Risk Assessment (RA)

To map robustness to handle the current cyber threats, start the RA process by assessing the systems onboard and ashore.

IT Department: Test and assess the IT & OT systems as follows:

  • Identify existing technical and procedural controls to protect both the vulnerable onboard and office IT & OT systems, the specific vulnerabilities, including human factors, and the policies and procedures governing these systems' use.
  • Identify and evaluate critical shipboard operations.
  • Identify possible cyber incidents, their impact on crucial shipboard operations, and the likelihood of their occurrence.
  • Prioritize and establish mitigating measures.
  • Perform periodic RAs by revisiting operating assumptions regarding capabilities and system monitoring needs.
  • Exercise due care and diligence concerning cybersecurity assets, risks, and protective systems, providing appropriate capabilities yielding protections deemed adequate against expected threats.
  • Incorporate all cybersecurity actions, automated systems, and risk management processes into a single Management System.

17.8.1            Activity Phases

Phase 1: Pre-assessment activities

Before a cybersecurity assessment:

  • Identify critical IT/OT & Communication systems.
  • Map the key functions and systems and their potential impact levels.
  • Identify primary providers of the critical IT & OT equipment.
  • Review detailed documentation of the critical OT & IT systems and their interfaces.
  • Identify cybersecurity points-of-contact at every provider and establish working relationships.
  • Review detailed documentation of the IT & OT systems maintenance and support.
  • Establish contractual requirements and obligations the Company may have for network and equipment maintenance and support.
  • Support RA with external experts to develop detailed plans and include makers and service providers.

 

 

Phase 2: Ship / Office assessment

The goal of assessing a ship's/Office's network and its systems and devices is to identify vulnerabilities that may lead to loss of service of the equipment, system, or network. These vulnerabilities and weaknesses may include:

  • Technical issues, such as software defects
  • Outdated or unpatched systems
  • Design issues, such as access management or implementation errors.

The activities must include:

  • A build and configuration review of computers, servers, routers, and firewalls
  • Reviews of all available cybersecurity documentation and procedures for connected IT/OT systems and devices.

Phase 3: Vulnerability review

  • Examine each identified vulnerability for its potential impact and probability of its exploitation.
  • Identify recommended technical and/or procedural corrective actions.

Phase 4: Provider debriefing

  • Send relevant findings to the providers of the affected systems.
  • Analyze the findings with external experts to achieve a full risk and technical understanding of the problem.
  • Ensure that the provider's remediation plan is comprehensive and the correct solution to eliminate the vulnerabilities is available.

17.8.2            Impact Assessment

The Confidentiality, Integrity, and Availability (CIA) model provides a framework for assessing the vulnerability to and the impact of:

  • Unauthorized access and disclosure of information or data about the ship, crew, cargo, and passengers
  • Loss of integrity, which would modify or destroy information and data relating to the ship's safe and efficient operation and administration
  • Loss of availability due to destruction of the information and data and/or the service/operation disruption of the ship's systems.

17.8.3            Reducing / Managing the Risk

The Company:

  • Uses a risk management method to contain and contextualize all cybersecurity and related risk issues into a risk Management System.
  • Seeks a sustainable and acceptable risk posture that is economical, feasible, and supportable.
  • Communicates information system and data risks relating to financial stability, brand reputation, and operations integrity in terms that its stakeholders understand.
  • Defines a risk tolerance strategy by monitoring the risk indicators supporting that strategy.
  • Links security controls to the compliance reporting requirements to indicate the degree of attainable security and not simple compliance.
  • Considers separately how to deal with occasions when the usual controls are invalidated, e.g.:
    • When there is no control over persons with access to onboard systems.
    • During dry-docking.
    • When taking over a new ship. It is impossible to know if malicious software is available in the onboard systems.
    • When third-party technicians connect via remote access for maintenance, reading system data, or troubleshooting.
    • When service providers or authorities connect removable media directly to an onboard system.

Cybersecurity defenses may be technical and focused on ensuring that onboard systems are resilient to cyberattacks. Company policies, safety management or security procedures, and access controls may also cover these defenses procedurally.

Both technical and procedural controls must be compatible with the CIA model for protecting data and information.

Prioritize the implementation of cybersecurity controls, focusing first on the defenses or combinations of defenses offering the most significant benefit.

17.9                    Human Resource Security

17.9.1            Employee Screening Check

The intention of employee screening is to minimize the cyber risk to the organization arising from accidental or deliberate malpractice, especially in critical cybersecurity roles.

The Company performs due care and due diligence when hiring new employees, particularly those that will operate or engaged in cybersecurity positions. The screening checks may include Cybersecurity work references, ICT academic and professional qualifications.

17.9.2            Employee Termination and Change of Employment

Upon employee’s termination, all software and hardware equipment provided by the Company must be returned in order to comply with the Company’s cybersecurity policy and procedures.

The following is an indicative return list of equipment:

  • Laptop/tablet
  • Mobile phone
  • Removable media (USBs, External Hard disks).

In Chapter 6 of the IMS the relevant forms include the software and hardware equipment on a specific role that has to be returned.

17.10               Asset Management

17.10.1       IT / OT and Communication Systems Inventory

A complete and accurate inventory of hardware and software information across the organization is the first step for a strong, robust, and mature cyber risk management system.

The Company keeps an up-to-date hardware and software inventory (form CS 001 and CS 002) for all IT, OT and Communication Asset Systems onboard and ashore in a way that:

  • Maps all cyber related critical assets.
  • Monitors the maintenance of critical systems.
  • Identifies and appoints Asset Owners.
  • Monitors the lifecycle of the equipment.
  • Monitors and controls the hardware and software deployment on its systems to:
    • Identify cybersecurity threats.
    • Evaluate existing cybersecurity controls.
    • Assess vulnerabilities including from third parties.
    • Perform qualitative RAs.

In Chapter 10 par. 10.2.5 and Appendix II of the IMS, the critical equipment related to cybersecurity are described.

17.10.2        IT / OT Acceptable Use Policy

All employees ashore & onboard:

  • You are expected to comply fully with all of the cybersecurity policies and procedures that are in place and to report any breaches of these policies of which they may become aware.
  • Anyone breaching the cybersecurity policy may be subject to disciplinary action.
  • Protect and use only their user credentials (user account and password, access token).
  • Access only IT/OT systems to which they have been given access.
  • Protect any classified material sent, received, stored or processed by you.
  • NOT attempt to bypass or subvert any IT/OT system cybersecurity controls or to use them for any purpose other than that intended.
  • DO NOT leave your computer unattended such that unauthorized access can be gained to office/ship’s IT/OT systems via your account.
  • DO NOT remove equipment or information from the office/ship’s premises without appropriate approval.
  • Inform immediately the CSO / Cybersecurity Company Officer ashore and/or Master / Cybersecurity Ship Officer onboard, if you detect, suspect or witness a cybersecurity incident that may be a breach of security or if you observe any suspected cybersecurity weaknesses in systems or services.
  • DO NOT introduce viruses or other malware into IT/OT systems or network.
  • DO NOT attempt to disable anti-virus protection provided at your computer or IT/OT systems.
  • You must always comply with the legal, statutory or contractual obligations relevant to your role.

17.10.3       Information Classification Procedure

The Company maintains inventories of all-important information and operation assets upon which it relies and protects the information it holds and processes by using classification controls appropriate to the sensitivity of the information involved.

This procedure sets out the details of the scheme to be adopted and the criteria applied in deciding which level of protection to apply to any given information asset.

This control applies to all information and operation systems, people and processes, including managers, employees, suppliers, contractors and other third parties who have access to the Company’s systems.

17.10.3.1     Classification Scheme

The classes of information are:

  • Public (or unclassified): Much of the information held by the Company is freely available to the public via established publication methods. Such items of information have no classification and will not be assigned a formal owner or inventoried.
  • Confidential: This is reserved for information which is highly sensitive and would cause major reputation and financial loss if it were lost or wrongly disclosed.

17.10.3.2     Information Labelling Procedure

In order to ensure that the correct controls are applied to the information and operation system assets, so that all employees and third parties (where applicable) are aware of how that information must be managed, the following system of protective marking may be used:

  • Printed Reports such as:
  • A watermark, clearly visible on every page of the document.
  • The classification is shown clearly on the front page and in the header of every page.
  • A stamp to mark each page with the security classification.
  • Screen Displays may include a warning:
  • Upon entering an area with a higher classification of information for saving or printing data.
  • Recorded Media with classified data are labelled externally with the security classification of the most sensitive data on the media.
  • Electronic Messages with classified information within:
  • Emails with sensitive or confidential information must include the classification level.
  • An attachment, the classification is clearly stated at the header of the document.
  • Classified File Transfers: The recipient is clearly informed of the classification level of the information being transmitted, before it is sent.

17.10.4       Management of Removable Media

Where removable media of any format (CD, DVD, memory stick, Media Card, External Hard Drives etc.) is used to store sensitive data, assess whether an alternative, more secure method can be used and if not, how best to secure the current method so that the risk is minimised.

Such methods may include:

  • Transfer of data to third parties e.g., suppliers, contractors, other agencies
  • Taking information home to work on
  • Backups of data in addition to scheduled server backups
  • Transfer of data between devices e.g., USB to ECDIS.

In the event that an existing method is not in the above list and contravenes the cybersecurity policy, identify an alternative method of achieving the desired end result.

The following tools can be supported by the IT Department:

  • Remote access via well-known relevant software
  • Encrypted memory stick

Where removable media is requested for legitimate purposes, use the following procedure.

17.10.4.1     User Request is Received

The IT Department will determine whether the use of removable media is the most appropriate method of achieving the business purpose that the user has.

17.10.4.2     Order New or Allocate Existing Removable Media

  • Use any new or re-usable removable media in stock in preference to ordering new.
  • Wipe any existing data in re-used removable media.
  • There is a protected spreadsheet that holds the following information about issued removable media:
    • Asset Number
    • Serial Number
    • Password
    • Allocated User
    • Date of issue.
  • Use the IT/OT inventory spreadsheet and create a new line for new removable media or find the correct line for re-issued removable media.

17.10.4.3     Set Removable Media Password

Always set a password for classified removable media. This must be at least 8 characters, have at least one capital letter and include a number.

IT Department: Provide the guidelines on how to do this.

17.10.4.4     Record Information in IT / OT Inventory Spreadsheet

Add the name of the allocated user to the spreadsheet and the date the removable media was issued.

17.10.4.5     Inform User of Key Facts

Email the user that has requested the removable media. If several have been requested, contact each person individually.

IT Department:

  • Where removable media are password protected, make the user aware that:
    • The data on the removable media may be fully encrypted.
    • The data WILL NOT be accessible without the password.
    • If the password is lost, the data WILL NOT be recoverable.
    • He MUST NOT write the password down or keep it with the removable media.
    • He MUST NOT change the password. If he does, the IT Support Desk will not be able to help him if he forgets it.
    • He must inform the IT Department if the removable media is lost.
  • Obtain email confirmation before the removable media is sent out that they have read and understood the above. Save the confirmation email on an IT shared drive.

17.10.4.6     Send Removable Media to User

  • Send the removable media to the user by internal post or deliver it by hand.
  • DO NOT include any passwords.

17.10.4.7       Provide User with Password in a Secure Way

  • Provide the password to the user by phone once they have received the removable media.
  • Verify the user’s identity.

17.10.5       Removable Media Policy

This policy defines the proper/expected usage of removable media (USB sticks, CDs/DVDs) in the Company's systems.

17.10.5.1     Security of Removable Media

Ashore

  • The use of unauthorized removable media devices is prohibited. Unauthorized devices are centrally blocked.
  • Transferring information to corporate PCs from third parties occurs via a dedicated “visitor” PC/laptop, using an authorized media device, with the IT Department's guidance. The “visitor’s” PC/laptop has no network connection.
  • Cameras and external hard disks are allowed only with the IT Department's authorization.
  • It is prohibited to charge mobile phones on corporate PCs.

All employees:

          Ensure the appropriate use and security of information stored in removable media devices.

          Store media in a safe place to minimize physical risk, loss, or theft.

          In case of loss, immediately inform the IT Department for their replacement.

          DO NOT use damaged or faulty removable media devices- request their replacement.

          Do not plug in unknown removable media devices into any system.

          Do not use company-owned removable media devices on personal machines or machines that do not belong to the company.

          Do not use personally owned removable media devices in company’s systems.

 

Onboard

  • DO NOT use unauthorized removable media devices on IT & OT equipment.
  • C/O and C/E: Ensure scanning of service engineers' USB sticks for viruses on a business PC/Laptop before plugging them into any system.
  • Block all USB ports on IT equipment for unauthorized removable media devices.
  • IT Department: Block the respective ports via a centralized platform, when applicable.
  • Block with protection covers all visible and accessible USB ports of the following OT equipment:
    • ECDIS Work Station 1 and Work Station 2
    • Cargo Monitoring System (if applicable)
    • VDR
    • Loadicator PC
    • Alarm Monitoring System.
  • Master and C/E:
  • Keep the above OT systems' USB ports blocked and unblock them only for business or troubleshooting purposes, using a special key in cooperation with the IT Department.
    • Request the replacement of any missing or damaged USB protection cover.
    • Distribute USB unblocking keys to the successors during a changeover.
    • Confirm this in handover checklists.
  • Transfer of information to ship's PCs from third parties occurs via a dedicated “visitor” PC using an authorized media device. “Visitor” PCs have no network connection.

 

DO NOT charge personal phones on ship equipment with USB ports.

17.10.5.2     Authorized Removable Media

  • Each ship may use authorized USB memory sticks, authorized hard disk, and authorized cameras. The list of authorized removable media, their purpose, and the person responsible are available in the following table:

 

Removable Media

Purpose

Responsible

Master USB memory stick

File transfer

Master

C/E USB memory stick

File transfer

C/E

ECDIS USB memory stick

Offline charts updates

Master

Ship camera

Photos transfer

C/E

 

  • Distribute authorized removable media to the successors during the handover process.
  • IT Department:
    • Configure the authorized USB sticks, where applicable, with password protection and with an embedded antivirus solution.
    • Update virus and malware checking software when you connect the removable media device to a networked IT PC.
  • Responsible crew:
    • Ensure the appropriate use and security of information stored in the authorized removable media devices.
    • Store media in a safe place to minimize physical risk, loss, or theft.

17.10.5.3     Disposal of Media

Log requests to securely dispose of media with the IT Department via telephone, email or online. The owner of the device must inform the IT Department for the need of the media disposal.

Provide the following details:

  • Requester name, role, department and contact details
  • The type of media to be disposed of
  • The serial number of the media and/or device containing the media (e.g., PC), if available
  • The classification of the information held on the media, if known
  • The location of the media
  • The reason for the media needing to be disposed of
  • When the media will be available for collection.

The owner of the device or media must ensure that any required backups have been made of the data prior to requesting disposal.

According to the type of media and the contractual arrangements with third parties, the IT Department will decide how best to dispose of the media, as following:

  • Local Disposal: Where available, local facilities will be used to securely dispose of certain types of media. Media that may be locally disposed of may include:
    • USB memory sticks
    • Hard disks
    • CDs and DVDs
    • Solid state storage devices
    • Floppy disks
    • Phones and tablets.

Only approved equipment e.g., a disk shredder may be used for local disposal.

  • Using a Third Party: For devices and media that require specialist equipment to securely destroy them a third party must be used.

17.11               Access control and Password Policy

17.11.1       Access Control ashore and onboard

  • Access is granted using the principle of ‘Least Privilege’.
  • Each user is identified by a unique user identity so that users can be linked to and made responsible for their actions.
  • The use of group identities is only permitted where they are suitable for the work carried out (e.g., training accounts or service accounts).
  • Records of user access will be used to provide evidence for security incident investigations.
  • Users have network access in accordance with the Company’s access control procedures and requirements defined by their roles.
  • Staff who access Company’s network remotely shall only be authenticated using the approved remote access authentication mechanism.

IT Department: Ensure that:

  • Diagnostic and configuration ports are only enabled for specified business reasons. All other ports are disabled or removed.
  • Network administrators group together information services, users and information systems as appropriate to achieve the required segregation on networks.
  • Only authorized personnel have access to system utilities. Access must be revoked when there is no longer a business reason for access.
  • All user workstations are configured to lock automatically after a period of inactivity to reduce the risk of unauthorized access.

All Company’s users:

  • Confirm that you are an authorized user at logon.
  • Have a unique identifier which MUST NOT be shared with other users.
  • Change your passwords at frequent intervals and in accordance with the password management policy.

17.11.1.1     User Registration and Deregistration

Account set up:

  • A request for access to the Company’s network and computer systems is submitted to the IT Department for approval. The principle of segregation of duties is applied.
  • During the initial creation of the user the below accounts are created:
    • Domain account
    • Mail Account – departmental
    • Departmental software (Danaos, Benefit, Task Assistant)
  • The system users do not have Administrative or Power User rights at the server or at any personal computer of the system. Thus, hardware and software installations can be held only by IT Department.
  • Access to systems sensitive applications (Performance Management System (PMS), Crewing Software, Accounting Software) is granted only to authorized users.
  • Users will be granted least amount of network access required to perform his or her job function according to the principles:
    • Need to know
    • Need to use
  • Accounts are implemented in a standard fashion and utilized consistently across the company.
  • Unique identiﬁers (IDs) provided to every user
  • Accounts are created using a standard format (i.e., first name. last name)
  • All accounts are password protected
  • Accounts are for individuals only. Account sharing, and group accounts are not permitted.
  • User accounts are not given administrator or 'root' access unless this is necessary to perform his or her job function.
  • Occasionally guests will have a legitimate business need for access to the corporate network. When a reasonable need is demonstrated, temporary guest access is allowed. This access, however, must be severely restricted to only those resources that the guest needs at that time, and disabled when the guest's work is completed.
  • The general principle «every action is prohibited unless expressly authorized» is applied.
  • An initial strong password is created on account setup and communicated to the user. The user is required to change the password.

 

Account use:

  • The company's standards dictate that username and password is an acceptable means of authentication as long as appropriate policies are followed.
  • User machines are configured to request authentication against the domain at startup.
  • Existing users on critical systems are reviewed semiannually to discover inactive users. “Review of Inactive Users” is also filled with the appropriate data and kept electronically on company’s server.
  • Remote access to the network can be provided for convenience to users but this comes at some risk to security. For that reason, the company encourages additional scrutiny of users remotely accessing the network. Remote access must adhere to the Remote Access section of this chapter.

 

Account Termination:

  • When managing network and user accounts, it is important to stay in communication with the Accounts and Office Personnel department so that when an employee no longer works at the company, that employee's account can be disabled. Human Resources must notify the IT Department in the event of a staffing change, which includes employment termination, employment suspension, or a change of job function (promotion, demotion, suspension, etc.).
  • Inactive users are removed of the system.
  • E-mail accounts are deactivated.

17.11.1.2     Removal or Adjustment of Access Rights

  • When a user is taking on a new role in addition to their existing one.
  • In case a user acquires a different role than the existing one.
  • Administrators are not permitted to change their own user accounts or permissions. 

17.11.1.3     Management of Privileged Access Rights

  • Privileged access rights such as those associated with administrator-level accounts are identified for each system or network and tightly controlled.
  • Admin level permissions are allocated to trained individuals whose roles require them.
  • Admin-level rights are provided only to individuals whose roles require them.

17.11.1.4     Employees Remote access

For the use of network communication equipment on non-company’s owned PCs or devices connected to the Company’s IT/OT systems the following are required:

  • Specific approval from the IT Department before connecting any equipment to the Company’s network.
  • Remote access to the network is implemented only via VPN connection. The request is always made via the IT Department.
  • The company will supply users with remote access software that allows for secure access and enforces the remote access policy.
  • Use of non-company-provided machines to access the corporate network is permitted, as long as this policy is adhered to, and as long as the machine meets the following criteria:
    • It has up-to-date antivirus software installed
    • Its software patch levels are current.

17.11.1.5     Contractors / Suppliers Access Ashore & Onboard

Physical access to equipment will require the appropriate approval and authorization by the appropriate department.

Contactors/suppliers must:

  • Comply with all applicable rules, policies and the company’s standards and agreements.
  • Use only the company’s information and Information resources for the purpose of the business agreement.
  • Report all security incidents directly to the company via agreed e-mail communication.
  • Report major work activities to the company.

IT Department:

  • Permission to connect to the Company’s network is mandatory. Maintain a log of activity.
  • DO NOT reveal details of how to access the Company’s network.
  • On termination or renewal of a contract, contractors or suppliers must immediately notify the IT Department so that the access can be updated or ceased. 
  • Manage all permissions and access methods.
  • Disable remote access software and remote user accounts when not in use.

Contractors / Suppliers onboard access:

  • Brief, accordingly, the Master / C/E on the work plan (tasks MUST NOT affect the operational status of the ship).
  • DO NOT access (physical or logical) any ship’s IT/OT & Communications equipment/system irrelevant to the work purpose. If needed, privileged access will be on a need to know basis under the supervision of the CySSO.
  • DO NOT carry and use any electronic equipment (i.e., Laptop, tablet, etc.) unrelated to the predefined tasks.
  • Conduct data transfer to ship’s IT/OT systems via a dedicated authorized ship’s media device. If the latter procedure is not applicable, use any necessary electronic equipment for the related task, which has been updated with the most recent patches and security requirements (malware free).
  • On work completion, debrief the Master/ CySSO, as applicable, with the deliverable, such as configuration/maintenance documentation, spare IT/OT parts and reassure them that tasks WILL NOT affect the operational status of the ship.

Contractors / Suppliers remote access:

  • Access to external vendors is allowed to specific systems in order for them to provide remote support on the Company’s business applications, as described in the respective maintenance and support contracts. The systems each vendor can connect to are pre-defined and restricted according to the support requirements.
  • In case contractors or suppliers would like to gain remote access to the Company’s network, they must inform the IT Department. In case of employment termination, the supplier must be immediately informed accordingly.
  • Use, where feasible, two factor authentication for:
  • Remote Network access
  • Remote System monitoring and maintenance.

17.11.1.6     Review of User Access Rights

On a regular basis (at least annually), asset and system owners are required to review who has access to their areas of responsibility and the level of access in place in order to identify:

  • People who must not have access (e.g., former employees)
  • User accounts with more access than required by their role
  • User accounts with incorrect role allocations
  • User accounts that do not provide adequate identification e.g., generic or shared accounts.

IT Department: Carry out a review of user accounts with privileged access regularly to ensure that this policy is being complied with.

 

17.11.2       Password Policy

17.11.2.1     Password generation

The Company, whether using single or multi-factor authentication, requires the quality of user passwords in all networks and systems to apply the following parameters:

 

Parameter

User Value

Minimum length

User: 8

System Administrator: 12

Maximum length

16

Re-use cycle

Cannot be the same as any of the previous 2 passwords

Characters Required

At least 1 capital letter - 1 symbol - 1 number

Change Frequency

Ashore: Every 6 months on Active Directory automatically

Onboard: Annually

Immediately when system is suspected to be compromised.

Account lockout
