Account must be re-enabled by IT Department

System Control

Checks above prerequisites and rejects incompatible passwords

Other controls

  • “Password Alternation Log” is filled with the appropriate data and kept electronically on company’s server.
  • Vendor default passwords change during system installation.

17.11.2.2     Password Confidentiality

  • Use a strong password in line with the rules set out in this policy.
  • DO NOT use dictionary words or acronyms.
  • Change the temporary password when connected to the system for the first time.
  • NEVER tell anyone your password or allow anyone else to use your account.
  • DO NOT record the password in writing or electronically e.g., in a file or email.
  • Avoid using the same password for other user accounts, either personal or business-related.
  • Ensure that any PC or device you leave unattended connected to the network is locked or logged out.
  • Leave nothing on display that may contain access information such as login names and passwords.
  • Inform the IT Department of any changes to your role and access requirements.
  • Password distribution is allowed via encrypted email. After delivery, email is deleted.
  • Onboard system passwords are available in an encrypted database, accessible only by the Master and the C/E. The Office updates the password database and distributes them automatically to all ships.
  • It is forbidden for the ship's crew to change the ship's systems' account passwords (IT or OT).

 

During a handover, the distribution of handover passwords must ensure their confidentiality.

17.12               Data Security

Data in transit or data in motion, is data actively moving from one location to another such as across the internet or through a private network. Data protection in transit is the protection of this data while it’s traveling from network to network or being transferred from a local storage device to a cloud storage device.

Data at rest is data stored on a hard drive, laptop, flash drive, or archived/stored in some other way. Data protection at rest aims to secure inactive data stored on any device or network.

The risk profile for data in transit or data at rest depends on the security measures that are in place to secure data in either state.

The Company implements the following controls for protecting its data ashore & onboard:

  • Maintains an inventory of sensitive systems.
  • Monitors and blocks unauthorized network traffic.
  • Only allows access to authorized cloud storage or email providers, where is used.
  • Manages and protects data on USB storage devices.
  • Manages system’s external removable media’s configurations.

Encryption plays a major role in data protection and is a popular tool for securing data both in transit and at rest. Encryption is seriously considered in the following scenarios:

  • On mobile devices such as laptops, tablets and smartphones
  • Where classified data is transmitted across communications lines like the Internet by using connections such as HTTPS, SSL, TLS, FTPS
  • For sensitive files prior to storing them and/or choose to encrypt the storage drive itself
  • For protection of data on removable media
  • For data storage in the cloud, if applicable
  • For systems password protection
  • For remote access on systems by using TLS for Virtual Private Networks.

It is vital that cryptographic keys are protected from modification, loss, destruction and unauthorised disclosure. A lifecycle approach will be taken to key management which will require the creation of specific procedures to cover the following stages:

  • Key generation
  • Distribution of keys to point of use
  • Storage at point of use
  • Backup as protection against loss
  • Recovery in the event of loss
  • Updating keys once expired
  • Revoking if compromised
  • Archiving once expired
  • Destroying when no longer required
  • Logging and auditing of key management related activities.

These procedures will take account of the specific circumstances in which encryption will be used.

17.13               Physical Security

This control applies to all systems onboard and ashore, people and processes that constitute the Company’s information IT/OT systems, including employees, suppliers and other third parties who have access to the Company systems.

17.13.1       Secure Areas

  • Physical security begins with the Ship/Office itself and an assessment of perimeter vulnerability is conducted. A Ship/Office has appropriate control mechanisms in place for the classification of information and equipment that is stored within it, such as:
    • Alarms fitted and activated outside working hours
    • Window and door locks
    • Access control mechanisms fitted to all accessible doors (where codes are utilized, they must be regularly changed and known only to those people authorized to access the area/building)
    • CCTV cameras
    • Protection against damage from e.g., fire, flood, vandalism.
  • Identification and access tools/passes (e.g., badges, keys, entry codes etc.).
  • Staff working in secure areas must challenge anyone not wearing a badge. Visitors to secure areas are required to sign in and out with arrival and departure times and are required to wear an identification badge.
  • An employee/seafarer escorts all visitors accessing secure areas at all times.
  • Where breaches do occur, or an employee/seafarer leaves outside normal termination circumstances, all identification and access tools/passes (e.g., badges, keys etc.) are recovered.

17.13.2       Working in Secure Areas

For all employees, third parties and other stakeholders who are given access to a secure area the following procedural instructions will apply.

Ashore & Onboard

  • Ensure you understand the specific instructions for all secure areas to which you are granted access.
  • DO NOT tell anyone about the secure area if you are requested not to.
  • Inform security of visitors you are expecting in time and escort them at all times.
  • DO NOT keep secure doors open for longer than necessary. NEVER allow anyone to tail-gate behind you through a secure entry point.
  • DO NOT work in the secure area on your own unless by prior arrangement.
  • NEVER lend anyone your ID badge or expose it to possible theft or loss. Challenge and/or report anyone not wearing an ID badge and remain vigilant whilst within the secure area.
  • DO NOT tell anyone your access PIN code or write your PIN code down.
  • Check vacant areas for signs of unauthorized access. Always ensure that doors and windows are secure before leaving if you are the last one out of the secure area.
  • The use of photographic, video or audio recording equipment is prohibited within the secure area unless by prior arrangement with the CSO / MASTER.
  • DO NOT leave classified information unattended in clear view of visitors.

17.13.3       Clear Desk & Clear Screen Policy

A Clear Desk & Screen Policy is a tool to ensure that all sensitive/confidential materials are removed from an end user workspace and locked away when the items are not in use or an employee leaves his workstation.

It is one of the top strategies to utilize when trying to reduce the risk of security breaches in the workplace. Such a policy can also increase employee’s awareness about protecting sensitive information.

Clear Desk Policy:

  • Where practically possible, store paper and computer media in suitable locked safes, cabinets or other forms of security furniture when not in use, especially outside working hours.
  • Where lockable safes, filing cabinets, drawers, cupboards etc. are not available, lock office doors if left unattended.
  • Store hard copy documents containing any personal data, or confidential, restricted or sensitive information only if necessary.
  • Secure all confidential, restricted or sensitive information in hardcopy or electronic form at the end of the day and when you are away from your desk for an extended period.
  • Remove any confidential, restricted or sensitive information from desks and lock them in a drawer when a desk is left unoccupied at any time.
  • Immediately clear from printers any confidential, restricted or sensitive information, when printed. Where possible, use printers with a ‘locked job’ facility.
  • Lock office areas when they are not in use and it is safe to do so.
  • Store any visit, appointment or message books in a locked area when not in use.
  • DO NOT keep any personally identifiable information on desks within reach or sight of visitors.
  • Store keys for desk drawers, cabinets and other secure areas in the dedicated key safe.
  • Remove any restricted or sensitive information from the desk and lock in a drawer when the desk is unoccupied and at the end of business day.
  • Immediately remove from the printer printouts containing classified information.
  • Use paper shredder equipment to destroy classified printouts.

Clear Screen Policy:

  • DO NOT leave computer terminals logged on when unattended.
  • Ensure computer terminals are password protected.
  • Ensure that computer screens are angled away from the view of unauthorized persons.
  • Log off computer workstations at the end of the working day, to allow security updates to be installed during the evening.
  • Set the Windows Security Lock to activate when there is no activity for a short pre-determined period of time.
  • Ensure that the Windows Security Lock is password protected for reactivation.
  • DO NOT leave passwords on sticky notes posted on or under a computer. DO NOT leave them written down or in an accessible location.
  • Log off or lock your machines (by pressing the Windows key and L) when you leave the room.
  • Erase whiteboards containing restricted and/or sensitive information.
  • Lock away any portable computing devices such as unused laptops, digital cameras and tablets in a drawer or the server room.
  • Mass storage devices such as CDROM, DVD or USB drives are sensitive data. Ensure they are locked away in a drawer or the server room.

17.13.4       Equipment Security

Ensure the following:

  • All general computer equipment is located in suitable physical locations that:
    • Limit the risks from environmental hazards, e.g., heat, fire, smoke, water, dust and vibration.
    • Limit the risk of theft e.g., if necessary, items such as laptops are physically attached to the desk.
    • Allow workstations handling sensitive data to be positioned so as to eliminate the risk of the data being seen by unauthorized people.
  • Data are stored on network file servers where available. This ensures that information lost, stolen or damaged via unauthorized access can be restored and its integrity maintained. 
  • All servers located outside of the data center are sited in a physically secure environment.
  • Business critical systems are protected by an Un-interruptible Power Supply (UPS) to reduce the operating system and data corruption risk from power failures.
  • In case of power outage the installed UPS can provide electricity for 40 minutes on the computer room.
  • Power Generator is able to supply power.
  • All items of equipment are recorded in the IT/OT asset inventory. Procedures are in place to ensure the inventory is updated as soon as assets are received or disposed of.

17.14               Management of Change Process

The objective of this process is to ensure that changes to IT/OT services and their associated components are recorded and then evaluated, authorized, prioritized, planned, tested, implemented, documented and reviewed in a controlled manner.

A change request:

  • May arise for many reasons, including the following:
    • An IT/OT incident or problem
    • New hardware & software installation, modification, removal or relocation
    • New IT & communication systems functionality
    • IT/OT Infrastructure upgrades
    • New or changed legislation
    • Retirement of service.
  • Must be assessed for impact (including information security implications) and resource requirements before being considered by the DPA.  To assist with impact assessment, the identification of related systems/components affected by the proposed change and also input from other affected support groups may be required. 
  • After assessment, if the change is deemed acceptable, it will be authorised by the DPA.
  • Once implemented, it will be reviewed and, subject to the findings of the review, closed.

The Company:

  • Retains an authorization process according to IMS Chapter 13 for IT/OT and communication systems that does not allow any unexpected, unattended, or unauthorized changes to critical systems or in operational systems that connect to critical systems.
  • Performs a formal, rigorous change & document control procedure critical to documenting IT/OT systems, maintaining knowledge of both, and implementing cybersecurity controls.
  • Maintains logs, system diagrams, and records for all business-critical or mission-critical systems that note the changes made during the change-control process.
  • When applicable, implements the parallel run model, which is a type of new system deployment testing where the new system and the old one are run in parallel. Each major or significant user/system process is performed on each system simultaneously to ensure that the new system supports all required business functionality that the old system supported or provided.

 

The Assets that fall under management of change procedure are included in the asset classification document.

 

Out of Scope

 

There are many IT services and tasks performed at the company, either by the IT department or by the end users that do not fall under the policies and procedures of Change Management. Services and tasks that require an operational process, but are outside the initial scope of Change Management process include:

  • Changes to non-production elements or resources
  • Changes made within the daily administrative process such are the below list.
    • Password resets
    • User adds/deletes
    • User modifications
    • Adding, deleting or revising security groups
    • Rebooting machines when there is no change to the configuration of the system
    • File permission changes

17.15               Cyber Defense

17.15.1       Types of Malware

Malware comes in many forms and is constantly changing as previous attack routes are closed and new ones are found. The most common types of malware found today are:

  • Macro viruses infect applications such as Microsoft Word or Excel.
  • File infectors usually attach themselves to executable code, such as .exe files. Another version of a file infector associates itself with a file by creating a virus file with the same name, but an .exe extension. Therefore, when the file is opened, the virus code will execute.
  • System or boot-record infectors: A boot-record virus attaches to the master boot record on hard disks. When the system is started, it will look at the boot sector and load the virus into memory, where it can propagate to other disks and computers.
  • Polymorphic viruses conceal themselves through varying cycles of encryption and decryption.
  • Stealth viruses take over system functions to conceal themselves.
  • Trojans is a program that hides in a useful program and usually has a malicious function. A major difference between viruses and Trojans is that Trojans do not self-replicate.
  • Logic bombs is a type of malicious software that is appended to an application and is triggered by a specific occurrence, such as a logical condition or a specific date and time.
  • Worms differ from viruses in that they do not attach to a host file, but are self-contained programs that propagate across networks and computers.
  • Droppers is a program used to install viruses on computers.
  • Ransomware is a form of malware designed to encrypt files on a device, rendering any files and the systems that rely on them unusable.

Often these types of malware are used in combination with each other.

17.15.2       How Malware Spreads

17.15.2.1     Phishing

This method involves tricking the user into taking some action that causes a malicious program to run and infect the computer being used. It is usually achieved via the blanket sending of unsolicited emails (Spam) with file attachments or web links included in them. When the user opens the file or clicks on the link the malicious action is triggered.

Phishing attacks can be very believable and enticing to the user. More targeted versions of phishing have appeared such as Spear Phishing (aimed at a particular organization) and even Whaling (aimed at an individual).

17.15.2.2     Websites and Mobile Code

The widespread use of mobile code such as JavaScript on websites has provided attackers with another route to infect computers with malware. Often websites will be created to host the malware which is activated either upon clicking on a link or in some cases simply by visiting the website.

Increasingly, legitimate websites are being compromised and made to host malware without the owner’s knowledge, making this type of attack very difficult for the user to avoid.

17.15.2.3     Removable Media

USB memory sticks, CDs, DVDs and other removable media devices provide an effective way of spreading malware onto additional computers. When the media is inserted into the machine the malware will either run and infect the target or will copy itself onto the removable media in order to prepare to infect the next machine it is plugged into.

17.15.2.4     Hacking

Hacking or “Cracking”, is a more targeted and therefore less common method of introducing malware onto a computer or network by gaining unauthorised access to the network from outside (and sometimes inside) the organization.

This method requires more knowledge on the part of the perpetrator and often exploits existing vulnerabilities in the software or network devices being used. Once access has been gained, malware will be installed remotely onto the compromised machine.

17.15.3       Anti - Malware Controls

The key concept adopted in this policy is “defence in depth” and no single control must be relied upon to provide adequate protection. This is a list of necessary controls, all of which are implemented where possible to guard against the threats outlined in the previous section.

17.15.3.1     Firewall

The Company installs a firewall(s) system at all points at which:

  • The internal ashore network is connected to the Internet.
  • The internal onboard network is connected to the Internet.
  • The Company’s office network is connected with the ship’s network.

Firewall Policy

  • All Firewall implementations adopt the position of "least privilege" and deny all inbound traffic by default.
  • Firewalls and network hardware provide secure administrative access (through the use of encryption) with management access limited, if possible, to only networks where management connections would be expected to originate.
  • No unnecessary services or applications are enabled on firewalls or routers.
  • Clocks on firewalls are synchronized with the company's other networking hardware using NTP or another means. Among other benefits, this will aid in problem resolution and security incident investigation.
  • Connections to the router or other network hardware are limited to the greatest extent possible. Exceptions to this are management connections that can be limited to known sources.
  • Firewalls include UTM capabilities such as intrusion detection systems and virus scanning software
  • The firewall ruleset is documented and reviewed semiannually. Audits must cover each rule, what it is for, if it is still necessary, and if it can be improved. Form “Firewall Ruleset and review” is also filled with the appropriate data and kept electronically on company’s server.
  • Firewall Rulesets and Configurations are backed up frequently to alternate storage.

17.15.3.2     Anti-Virus / Endpoint Protection

The Company:

  • Safeguards endpoints or entry points of end-user devices such as desktops, laptops, and mobile devices from being exploited by malicious actors and campaigns.
  • Protects the endpoints from malware spreading via removable media.
  • Identifies and prevents cyberattacks from sophisticated malware and evolving zero-day threats.
  • Controls and monitors external removable devices (i.e., USB’s, external hard disks).
  • Ashore uses Akereon as e-mail provider and Wingu client for message communications while onboard uses GTMailPlus –GTMaritime.
  • Ensures that:
    • All company-provided user workstations have antivirus/anti-malware software installed listed in Premises Asset Classification.
    • Ships are protected with antivirus listed in Ships Asset Classification.
    • On premises antivirus is managed from the Management console.
    • Patches, updates, and antivirus signature file updates are installed in a timely manner, either automatically or manually.
    • On premises antivirus are updated automatically.
    • Antivirus on ships with terminal server are updated weekly on other occasions are updated with CD.
    • Onboard:
      • E-mail client is installed on ships bridge
      • Bridge PC is password protected and mail client has log in management capabilities.
      • E-mail is accessed physically or through RDP from captain cabin per case.
      • E-mail is protected from spam e-mail and viruses through the protection mechanisms of the e-mail provider.

 

Malware Defense

          Utilize centrally managed anti-malware software.

          Ensure anti-malware software signatures are updated.

          Enable operating system (OS) anti-exploitation features/deploy anti-exploit technologies.

          Configure anti-malware scanning of removable media.

          Centralize anti-malware logging for analysis and alerting.

          Enable command-line audit logging.

17.15.3.3     Email Filtering

The Company installs a system (physical or cloud solution) which:

  • Filters out unsolicited and potentially harmful emails (spam).
  • Blocks or removes attachments containing malware before delivery to the user.
  • Filters suspicious mail fishing links which are blocked or removed when malware is detected.

17.15.3.4     Web Content Filtering

Web content filtering is the practice of blocking access to web content that may be deemed offensive, inappropriate, or even dangerous.

The Company installs a hardware or software-based Content Filtering solution which:

  • Establishes rules about the types of visited internet sites.
  • Prohibits access to pornographic, drug, alcohol, gambling and other malicious sites.
  • Uses keywords or other commonalities between sites so as to group content into categories - such as gambling and human trafficking.

17.15.3.5     Ransomware Protection

The Company takes into serious consideration ransomware threat by using where applicable, below counter measures:

  • Maintains offline, backups of data and regularly tests the backups.
  • Maintains updated “gold images” of critical systems in case they need to be rebuilt.
  • Creates, maintains, and exercises a basic cyber incident response plan and associated communications plan that includes response and notification procedures for a ransomware incident.

 

Infection Vectors

Internet:

  • Conduct regular vulnerability scanning to identify and address vulnerabilities.
  • Regularly patch and update software and operating systems to the latest available versions.
  • Ensure devices are properly configured and that security features are enabled.
  • Employ best practices (i.e., multifactor authentication, strong passwords) for use of RDP and other remote desktop services.
  • Disable or block Server Message Block (SMB) protocol outbound and remove or disable outdated versions of SMB

Phishing:

  • Implement a cybersecurity user awareness and training program that includes guidance on how to identify and report suspicious activity or incidents.
  • Apply filters at the email gateway to filter out emails with known malicious indicators.
  • Consider disabling macro scripts for Microsoft Office files transmitted via email.

Precursor Malware Infection:

  • Ensure antivirus and anti-malware software and signatures are up to date.
  • Use only authorized software.
  • Consider implementing an intrusion detection system (IDS) to detect command and control activity.

Third Parties: Consider the Company’s risk management to meet its mission.

17.15.4       Vulnerability Management

The Company ashore and onboard:

  • Collects information on software vulnerabilities from vendors and third-party sources and updates applied where available.
  • If possible, updates are applied automatically as soon as they are released.
  • Performs vulnerability scanning regularly, particularly on business-critical IT/OT systems and networks.

17.15.5       Threat Monitoring and Alerts

Information about cyber emerging threats is obtained from various sources. Users are alerted proactively of potential attacks, via regular training, campaigns, posters and drills.

17.16               User Awareness & Training

The personnel have a crucial role in protecting IT and OT systems ashore and onboard. Training and awareness must match the appropriate levels for:

  • Onboard personnel, including the Master, Officers, and crew
  • Shoreside personnel, supporting the ship's management and operation.

A training program is available for all personnel, covering at least the following:

  • Risks related to:
    • Emails and safe behavior
    • Internet usage, including social media, chat forums, and cloud-based file storage
    • Use of removable media and personal devices.
  • Installing and maintaining software on the Company's hardware using infected hardware (removable media) or software (infected package)
  • Safeguarding user information and passwords
  • Cyber risks concerning the physical presence of non-Company personnel, i.e., where third-party technicians work on equipment without supervision
  • Detecting suspicious activity or devices and reporting procedures for a potential cyber incident
  • Awareness of the consequences or impact of cyber incidents on the ship's safety and operations
  • Understanding the implementation of preventative maintenance routines, such as antivirus and antimalware, patching, backups, and incident response planning and testing
  • Protection procedures against risks from service providers' removable media before connecting to the ship's systems
  • Cybersecurity related International regulatory and Industry references.

The Company promotes cybersecurity awareness to all staff by various actions, i.e.:

  • Onboard presentation and discussion with crew during ICT attendances.
  • Cybersecurity training records are being kept whenever training takes place.
  • Discussion with on-signers during briefing procedures.
  • Notifications, bulletins, and instruction emails that are systematically being sent by the IT Department to the ships and to the office users.
  • Posters promoting Cybersecurity.
  • Training sessions by third party security consultants.

17.17               IT / OT Software & Hardware Management

This procedure sets out how hardware and software of IT/OT and Communication systems ashore and onboard will be acquired, tested, installed and supported within the Company.

17.17.1       Purchasing

IT Department:

  • Follow corporate general purchasing procedures.
  • Ensure equipment compliance with safety and cybersecurity regulations.
  • Ensure supplier provides licenses, download links or installation disks, and instructions.

OT software comes with the equipment it monitors and controls, so there is no need for formal acquisition requests and approvals.

17.17.2       Testing

  • Before deploying any software or hardware, the IT Department ensures that its operation does not affect the existing systems' and services' integrity.
  • Test, using demo licenses, all new IT and OT software or software upgrades for correct operation and compatibility with current infrastructure.

 

17.17.3       Installation

  • Any new installation is permitted only with the approval and supervision of the IT team and if needed by the appropriate Manager.
  • Licensed software will be installed by the IT Department or appropriate technical team of a contractor or supplier upon request with special caution on OT systems.
  • The user is not allowed to install any hardware of IT/OT system.
  • IT Department uses only white listed application.
  • The user is not allowed to install any software that is licensed to them personally, whether or not it is free, shareware or commercial:
    • If a user tries to install a new program, a pop-up window appears on the screen requesting administrator credentials.
    • Only the IT Coordinator has these credentials.

The Company has removed all administrative privileges from all users through its main Administrative Control.

17.17.4       Maintenance

Maintenance during the system's lifecycle is necessary to maximize operating efficiency and minimize security issues. For all the IT/OT assets, the Company:

  • Gets the latest applicable upgrades/updates.
  • Maintains contracts with vendors or suppliers.

Software updates provide solutions for features that are not working as intended (bugs) or add enhancements to resolve compatibility issues. They also include device driver updates.

 

Software upgrades refer to new versions of software that provide major/significant changes (inclusion/removal of features) over the current version.

  • OT systems: The vendor of equipment provides information about available updates/upgrades.
  • IT systems: Feedback is coming by email notifications directly from software providers.

 

Malware Defense:

          Catalog hardware configurations, software holdings and licenses to prioritize and apply patches.

          Test system’s application patches on a testbed before applying to operational systems.

          Restrict software from running unless it concerns tested and approved software (whitelisting).

          Document any new changes to systems.

 

Vendor / Contractor / Supplier Support Team:

  • Perform ICT system software upgrades or deployment.
  • Especially on ships, the installation files must get to the systems onboard. Depending on the size of setup, the scope of installation (specific ship, whole fleet), and the criticality of deployment, the installation files can be transferred through media storage disks (physical transfer) or by communication links (through satellite).
  • When the files are onboard, a member of the IT Department proceeds with the software installation remotely or provides installation instructions to the Master.

IT Department:

  • Perform ICT system software upgrades or deployment.
  • For each item of software, a master copy of any media, enabling codes and installation instruction is stored safely.
  • Especially on ships, the installation files must get to the systems onboard. Depending on the size of setup, the scope of installation (specific ship, whole fleet), and the criticality of deployment, the installation files can be transferred through media storage disks (physical transfer) or by communication links (through satellite).
  • When the files are onboard, a member of the IT Department proceeds with the software installation remotely or provides installation instructions to the Master.

Master:

  • In cases where a customized setup is pre-configured by the IT Department (through a "runasp" executable), proceed with the installation directly. In such cases, the setup folder also includes a document (doc/pdf) with detailed step-by-step installation instructions.
  • Following a new software deployment (or upgrade of an existing one), performance tests define if the software performs as expected, i.e., Disk I/O, CPU/RAM utilization, network latency, monitoring possible deviations.
  • Finally, verify the product's installed version by visually checking that the application's update/upgrade to the desired version (through the Help/About menu dialogs or the Programs and features list, etc.) was successful.

The Company for all its IT/OT software and hardware equipment:

  • Retains all copies of manufacturer’s instructions.
  • Identifies recommended service intervals and specifications.
  • Enables a call-out process in case of failure.
  • Ensures only authorized technicians complete any work on the equipment.
  • Records details, if possible, of all remedial work carried out.
  • Records details, if possible, of faults incurred and actions required.
  • Maintains a service history record of equipment so that decisions can be made regarding the appropriate time for it to be replaced.
  • Ensures that manufacturer’s maintenance instructions are documented and available for support staff to use when arranging repairs.
  • If the equipment is to be passed onto another/into the Company (e.g., ship acquisition), data removal must be achieved by using approved, appropriately secure software tools.

17.17.5       Removal

Ensure the following:

  • Management of Change and relevant RA is prepared and submitted before proceeding with software/hardware removal.
  • Software/Hardware removal is performed in the production environment.
  • Equipment that is to be disposed must have all of its data erased/destroyed.
  • A new revision of the ICT Software/Hardware Inventory is prepared by removing the relevant record.
  • When a software program is no longer required, the IT Department is informed.
  • Software licenses from removed systems may be reused by the IT Department.
  • Users MUST NOT remove licensed software from corporate devices.

17.17.6       Backup policy

The purpose of this policy is to provide means to:

  • Restore the integrity of the IT/OT systems in the event of a hardware/software failure or physical disaster.
  • Provide a measure of protection against human error or the inadvertent deletion of important files.

 

Ashore:

  • All user-level and system-level information maintained by the Company is backed up using Altaro at QNAP System. The backup media is stored with sufficient protection and proper environmental conditions.
  • The frequency of backups is in accordance with the importance of the information and the acceptable risk as determined by the data owner, currently every day with retention period 7 days.
  • The information resources backup and recovery process for each system is documented and periodically reviewed.
  • Geographic separation from the backups is maintained. The in-house company’s backup is kept on separate floor inside the premises.
  • The company implements Disaster Recovery (DR) Site in remote location independent on different building of the company. DR back up is scheduled daily at 12 at night. System is replicated in remote site using VPN. The company is able to recover the IT server infrastructure at all times.
  • Physical access controls implemented at offsite backup storage locations meet or exceed the physical access controls of the source systems. Additionally, backup media are protected in accordance with the highest sensitivity level of information stored.
  • The system backup information is provided with protection from unauthorized modification and environmental conditions.
  • Backups every 6 months are tested to ensure that they are recoverable. The appropriate record is presented in Form “Backup Tests” which is kept electronically on company’s server.
  • Procedures between the Company and the offsite backup storage vendor(s) are (if applicable) reviewed at least annually.

 

Onboard:

  • All data determined to be critical to company operation and/or employee job function.
  • All information stored on network servers, which may include web servers, database servers, domain controllers, firewalls, and remote access servers and corporate file server(s).
  • Critical Operating Systems
  • Terminal Server is backed up daily.

17.18               Network Security

17.18.1       Network Documentation

Network documentation, specifically as it relates to security, is important for efficient and successful network management. Further, the process of regularly documenting the network ensures that the company has a firm understanding of the network architecture at any given time.

Network documentation includes:

  • Network diagrams for premises and ships
  • Access Control Lists – Active Directory.

The company requires that network documentation to reviewed and updated on an annual basis or after significant changes.

17.18.2       Network Segregation

Where appropriate, a network will consist of a set of smaller networks segregated from each other based on either trust levels or organizational boundaries (or both). 

For a large network this is achieved using separate domains, particularly where separate organizations’ networks are being linked. An appropriate level of trust is configured at the domain level and domain perimeters are secured using a firewall where appropriate.

Within networks, Virtual Local Area Networks (VLANs) will be used to segregate organizational units.

The company confirms that security architecture protecting the existing systems, facilities, personnel and assets is adequately replicated in terms of functions during a disaster recovery scenario.

Onboard best practice guide:

  • Create an IDMZ to completely separate the Business and Crew networks from all OT networks.
  • Use data diodes as single direction gateways preventing malicious code entering the OT network from IT compromised devices.
  • Create Business and Crew VLANs to segregate high risk devices, such as unmanaged BYOD and crew laptop.
  • Consider using different color ethernet cabling for every VLAN.
  • Avoid putting any hosts on the default VLAN (VLAN 1).
  • Enable explicit tagging of the Native VLAN for all trunk ports.
  • Use of dedicated switch with different VLANs for OT systems, where possible.
  • Avoid Inter-VLAN routing.
  • If applicable, use Vitrual Access Control Lists (VACLs) to filter traffic within a VLAN, otherwise use extended ACLs.

In a cloud environment, ensure that requirements for segregating networks to achieve tenant isolation are defined and the cloud service provider’s ability to meet these requirements is verified.

Figure 1 Ship Network Architecture Diagram (BIMCO Workbook, 3rd Edition 2022)

Ashore best practice guide:

  • Create VLANs per Department.
  • Consider creating Guest VLAN for onsite or remote third party’s access.
  • Consider using different color ethernet cabling for every VLAN.
  • Avoid putting any hosts on the default VLAN (VLAN 1).
  • Enable explicit tagging of the Native VLAN for all trunk ports.
  • Where applicable, avoid Inter-VLAN routing (e.g., third parties VLAN for remote maintenance).
  • If applicable, use VACLs to filter traffic within a VLAN, otherwise use extended ACLs.

In a cloud environment, ensure that requirements for segregating networks to achieve tenant isolation are defined and the cloud service provider’s ability to meet these requirements is verified.

 

Securing OT Systems:

          Implement Network Segmentation – IDMZ.

          Backup all OT software.

          Harden devices by:

o         Update-patch systems

o         Change default passwords

o         Restrict and review user permissions and accounts regularly

o         Disable unnecessary features.

          Collect logs, where feasible via a Security Information and Event Management System (SIEM).

          Get automatic alerts by email.

          Restrict physical access (blockout devices, lock-in cables).

          Maintain hygiene life cycle.

17.18.3       Perimeter Security & Resilience

At all perimeters between the internal network and an external network (such as the Internet) effective measures are in place ensuring that only authorised network traffic is permitted.

This will usually consist of at least one Stateful Inspection firewall and for major links with the Internet an Application (or Application Gateway) firewall must be used. For connections such as broadband at smaller locations, a Packet Filtering firewall may suffice, depending on the results of a RA. 

Servers that are intended to be accessed from an external, insecure network (such as web servers) are located in a Demilitarised Zone (DMZ) of the firewall.

Onboard

  • In case the ships firewall / accounts and network interfaces are managed by a communication provider or other 3rd party the company should have administrative access to audit the firewall configuration and operation.
  • Connection from the premises to ships servers should be performed with a secure connection (VPN). The company uses VNC and RDP for remote connection to the ships. Only Whitelisted IP from the premises are permitted to connect.
  • Remote access for ships is implemented as below:
    • Through VNC client from the company’s premises. Only the company’s IP address is able to access the ship.
    • Through dedicated secure portal
    • Via SSH
  • Using a different satellite (such as VSAT and FBB) or 4G/5G with shore-side network in order to provide redundancy for the data and voice communication of the ship.
  • SatCom/4G/5G network providers are configured in an Active-Active fail-safe mode.

Ashore

  • Rules have been set up on the shore side Inmarsat Service Provider firewall equipment in order to allow only authorized data traffic to/from the ship, bound to specific source/destination IPs and ports.
  • The email service onboard is provided by a third party. The ship’s workstations connect via a secure channel (whitelisted IP addresses) to the servers ashore for email exchange to take place. Apart from the email service, antivirus, anti-phishing, and archiving services could be provided.

 

Secure Configuration Requirements for Network Devices:

          Maintain standard security configurations.

          Document traffic configuration rules.

          Use automated tools to verify standard device configuration and detect changes.

          Install the latest stable version of any security-related updates on all network devices.

          Manage network devices using multi-factor authentication and encrypted sessions.

          Use dedicated workstations for all network administrative tasks.

          Manage network infrastructure through a dedicated network.

17.18.4       Public Networks

For information transferred over a public network such as the Internet, strong encryption via SSL/TLS is used to ensure the confidentiality of the data transmitted.

17.18.5       Wi-Fi Networks

Ashore & Onboard

  • The Service Set Identifier (SSID) of the access point is changed from the factory default.
  • Access points without user authentication are forbidden.
  • Default passwords change immediately after the installation of new wireless access points.
  • Encryption is used to secure wireless communications. Stronger algorithms are preferred to weaker ones.
  • Access point should enforce wireless client isolation.
  • Wi-Fi transmission range should be limited to the company’s premises.
  • Wireless access points are configured to not broadcast their Service Set Identifier (SSID) and to not allow secure connection using WPS (Wi-Fi Protected Setup) via physical access to the access point itself.

17.18.6       Physical Security

Ashore & Onboard

  • Remote network equipment is housed in secure cabinets which is locked at all times. Only support staff has access to the key to each cabinet.
  • Critical or sensitive network equipment, where applicable will be housed in an environment that has a monitored temperature and backup power supply.
  • Critical or sensitive network equipment is protected by fire suppression systems.
  • Backbone and centralized network equipment is in appropriate lockable cabinets or racks in a secure server room to which only authorized support staff has access.
  • Where possible, wireless access points located in public areas are hidden from view.
  • Lockable protective casing protects access points if located in an unprotected public area e.g., deck area.
  • All visitors to secure network areas must be authorized.
  • Entry to secure areas housing critical or sensitive network equipment is restricted to those whose job requires it.

17.18.7       Network Intrusion Detection

  • A Network-based Intrusion Detection System (NIDS) can be installed at the network perimeter and at all key points within the network e.g., on critical servers.
  • For critical IT/OT networks with high security requirements, consider an Intrusion Prevention System (IPS).

17.18.8       Logging and Monitoring

Company’s network infrastructure is monitored 24/7/365 by external service provider using SIEM (Security Information Event Management) and logs from workstations and servers are kept for 2 months.

17.18.9       Network Changes

  • All changes to network devices are subject to the MoC process.
  • Update configuration records whenever such changes are carried out.

17.18.10  Video Conference Policy

The Company uses Zoom Video Conferencing software to fulfill its business needs. The following rules apply:

  • All usernames are unique and managed by the appointed account Administrator.
  • Personal, non-corporate accounts are strictly prohibited.
  • File transfer of confidential data is prohibited.
  • Messages transmitted through a session (i.e., Skype) are automatically encrypted from end to end.
  • Recording of Video or VOIP calls are permitted depending on the sensitivity of the conference.
  • Recording of presentations are allowed depending on the terms agreed for each presentation.

17.18.11  Internet Acceptable Use Policy

The purpose of this Policy is to:

  • Provide employees with rules and guidelines about the appropriate use of Internet access.
  • Protect both the Company and the employee. The employee must be aware that:
    • Browsing certain sites or downloading files is prohibited.
    • The policy must be adhered to or there could be serious repercussions, thus leading to fewer security risks as a result of employee negligence.

 

Company’s employees: You must abide by the following rules:

  • You must use the internet including social media, chat forums etc., responsibly. 
  • All internet data that is composed, transmitted and/or received by the Company’s computer systems is considered to belong to the employer and to be part of the Company’s official data. It is therefore subject to disclosure for legal reasons to authorized third parties. This also applies to sharing or transmitting data, including but not limited to files, photos and text information, taken offline that was acquired from the Company’s computer systems.
  • The Company reserves the right to monitor internet traffic and access data that is composed, sent or received through its online and local network connections.
  • Data sent, downloaded or received via the Company’s internet system MUST NOT contain content that is deemed to be offensive, provocative or distasteful. This includes, but not restricted to the use of vulgar or socially unacceptable or discriminatory language/images regarding age, race, sex, national origin, disability, religion, culture, medical condition and sexual orientation.
  • Data sent, downloaded or received via the Company’s internet system may be blocked by the IT Department if deemed to contravene this Policy and/or be harmful to the business.
  • Internet is to be used in accordance with local national laws and regulations. The downloading of any inappropriate, illegal or offensive material is strictly prohibited.
  • You MUST NOT:
    • Send or post discriminatory, harassing or threatening messages or images on the internet, including social media, chat forums etc.
    • Use devices to perpetrate software, film or music piracy.
    • Disclose someone else's personal information.
    • Violate copyright laws, download or copy software and electronic files.
    • Share confidential material, photos of work areas, trade secrets, or proprietary information relating to the Company.
    • Hijack devices or hack into accounts.
    • Send or post information that is defamatory to the employer, its services, employees and/or customers/contractors.
    • Post or exchange confidential Company’s information and/or disclose corporate information that is not public.
    • Introduce malicious software onto the Company’s computer network and/or jeopardize the security of the Company’s electronic communications systems.
    • Write, copy, execute or attempt to introduce any computer code designed to replicate, damage or otherwise hinder the performance of or access to any of the Company’s computers, networks or data.
    • Send or post chain letters, solicitations or advertisements not authorized by the Company.
    • Communicate personal views as representing those of the Company.
    • Abuse, exploit or damage any internet or local network connected devices.
    • Conduct fraudulent or illegal activities, including but not limited to gambling, trafficking in drugs or weapons or participating in terrorist propaganda or acts.
    • Perform any act that may defame, abuse, embarrass, tarnish or portray a negative image of the Company, employees, or any other party related to the Company.
  • If unsure about what constitutes acceptable internet usage, ask the Company for further guidance and clarification.

17.19               Email Security

This section defines the rules and guidelines for the proper and secure use of corporate email which must be used only for business purposes.

17.19.1       Use of E-mail Systems and Prohibited Actions

Users are asked to exercise common sense when sending or receiving email from company accounts. Additionally, the following applies to the proper use of the company email system.

  • When using a company email account, email must be addressed and sent carefully. Users should keep in mind that the company loses any control of email once it is sent external to the company network.
  • Users must take extreme care when typing in addresses, particularly when email address auto-complete features are enabled using the "reply all" function; or using distribution lists in order to avoid inadvertent information disclosure to an unintended recipient. Careful use of email will help the company avoid the unintentional disclosure of sensitive or non-public information.
  • The following are never permitted:
    • Send any emails that may cause embarrassment, damage to reputation, or other harm to the company.
    • Spamming
    • Harassment
    • communicating threats
    • solicitations
    • chain letter
    • send any information that is illegal under applicable laws.
    • Conduct non-company-related business
    • Make fraudulent offers for products or services.
  • Users are prohibited from sending business email from a non-company-provided email account.

This list is not exhaustive but is included to provide a frame of reference for types of activities that are prohibited.

  • The company may take steps to report and prosecute violations of this policy, in accordance with company standards and applicable laws.
  • Additionally, users are asked to recognize that email sent from a company account reflects on the company, and, as such, email must be used with professionalism and courtesy.
  • Users should never open unexpected email attachments or email attachments from unknown sources and click links within email messages unless he or she is certain of the link's safety
  • Users are permitted to access external or personal email accounts from the corporate network, as long as such access does not negatively impact the user's job performance
  • Monitoring and Privacy: Users should expect no privacy when using the corporate network or company resources. Such use may include but is not limited to: transmission and storage of files, data, and messages. The company trusts its employees and respects their privacy; therefore, it does not monitor any of their email communications conducted over their business email account.
  • For security purposes all executables, macros and scripts attached on emails are filtered. All emails are scanned twice, once on the company’s firewalls and once on its mail server.
  • The Email system allows sending/receiving emails with content up to 25 MB.
  • A disclaimer is used when sending emails from Company addresses to recipients outside the Company.
  • Users are advised to avoid using third-party email systems, such as Google, Yahoo, and MSN Hotmail, to conduct Company business, to create any binding transactions, or to store and retain emails on behalf of the Company.
  • Where possible, use links to files instead of attaching files to emails to avoid mailboxes filling up.

17.19.2       Spam Email Procedures

If the user received a suspicious email usually from an unknown sender but and from a known sender with suspicious subject they should perform the following actions:

  • Read the subject of the email. If the email’s subject seems legitimate and work related, then the user shall proceed to the next action, otherwise move it in the spam mail folder.
  • Carefully verify the sender's email address. The user should search it on the internet in order to verify it, or even call the sender’s company/premise to verify its authenticity. If the email address is verified then the user should proceed to the following step, otherwise move it in the spam mail folder.
    • An email address (e.g. someone@company.word) consists of three parts
    • Someone: the name of the sender
    • Company: the name of the domain
    • Word: the name of the top-level-domain

 In this example the “@company.word” should be verified.

  • Hash busting: using special characters designed to break up words or phrases (e.g. “Fr3e W!nn@r”).
  • Bad links: Avoid linking to unreputable sites or content, or using url shorteners.
  • Misleading subject lines: using “Re:” or “Fwd:” when you’ve never communicated with a recipient before.
  • Sloppy html code: Using Microsoft Word to design in html can add extra formatting to the code, which raises your spam score (and also makes your emails look terrible).
  • Too much image, not enough text: embedding text inside of images or sending emails that are all-image, no text.
  • Using all-caps WHEN it’s not NECESSARY: makes your message seem salesy and possibly suspicious.
  • The user should be very careful with any internet links, buttons and/or images on the email’s body and he/she should avoid to open them if possible.

17.19.3       Email Ownership

Users should be advised that the company’s Managing Director owns and maintains all legal rights to its email systems and network, and thus any email passing through these systems is owned by the company and it may be subject to use for purposes not be anticipated by the user.

17.19.4       E-mail Administration

  • Email addresses must be constructed in a standard format in order to maintain consistency across the company.
  • E-mail account creation and termination is covered by Network Access and Authentication.
  • Akereon keeps e-mail logs 10 days for outgoing messages and 3 days for incoming messages
  • Akereon Mail server keeps mails for 30 days maximum
  • MDeamon keeps e-mails forever.

 

If at any point the user is not sure for the legitimacy of an email then he/she should immediately seek help from the IT department.

17.20               Incident Response and Recovery Plan

17.20.1       Cyber incident & Contact Details

A loss of IT systems, including a data breach of confidential information, would be a business continuity issue and would normally not have immediate, significant impact on the safe operation of the ship.

The loss of OT systems may have a significant and immediate impact on the safe operation of the ship.

 

Should a cyber incident result in the loss or malfunctioning of OT systems, take actions to guarantee the immediate safety of crew, ship, cargo and the protection of the environment.

 

Regardless of other incidents, cyber incidents may result in multiple failures causing more systems to shut down at the same time.

 

In the event of a cyber incident (in IT or OT systems) notify the Company and immediately implement the response and recovery plans, as described in the following sections.

17.20.2       Detecting and reporting a cyber incident

The use of monitoring and reporting systems, where possible, help identify ongoing threats. Other methods of detecting a cyber incident include:

IT Systems:

  • Unusual password activity, e.g., an unexpected prompt to change a password
  • Suspicious pop-ups or adware, especially when browsing the Internet
  • Unexpectedly slow or unresponsive systems or network
  • Clear evidence of a virus or system breach, e.g., a demand for ransomware payment, detection of a physical device, such as a key logger
  • Email/Communication failure
  • Ship Server breakdown.

          Report cyber security incidents on IT systems, actual or suspected, to IT Department and the CySSO immediately. Provide as much information and details as possible. Include screenshots, if possible.

          Master: For ship communication issues you may contact the communication vendor directly. Include IT Department in any email communication.

 

OT Systems:

  • The engine slow down unexpectedly (especially on a risk area)
  • The bridge team have concluded that the navigation systems are no longer trustworthy or loss of availability of electronic navigational equipment
  • Unexpectedly slow or unresponsive systems or network
  • Loss of essential connectivity with the shore, including but not limited to the availability of GMDSS communications
  • Loss of availability of industrial control systems, including propulsion, auxiliary systems and other critical systems, as well as loss of integrity of data management and control
  • Unauthorized access to critical systems
  • Unauthorized connection of removable media or personal devices.

 

In case of cyber security incidents on OT critical systems, notify the Company’s ERT, in order for the ERP to get started.

 

Report actual or suspected cyber security incidents on OT systems to the Technical/Marine S/T and the CySCO immediately. Provide as much information/details as possible. Include screenshots, if possible.

17.20.3       Prioritizing cyber incidents

Cyber incidents are not handled on a first-come, first-served basis as a result of resource limitations. Instead, they are prioritized based on the relevant factors, such as the following:

Functional impact of the Incident: Incidents targeting Company’s systems typically impact the business functionality that those systems provide, resulting in some type of negative impact to their users.

 

 

Category

Definition

Low

Minimal, if any effect. The Company can still provide all critical services to all users but has lost efficiency.

Medium

The Company has lost the ability to provide a critical service to a subset of system users.

High

The Company is no longer able to provide some critical services to any users.

Critical

Several critical systems have been compromised and are inoperable.

 

Information impact of the Incident: Incidents may affect the confidentiality, integrity, and availability of the Company’s information. Incident handlers must consider how this information extraction will impact the Company’s overall mission.

 

Category

Definition

No impact

No information was extracted, changed, deleted, or otherwise compromised.

Privacy Breach

Sensitive personally identifiable information (PII) of employees, beneficiaries, etc. was accessed or extracted.

Proprietary Breach

Unclassified proprietary information, such as protected critical infrastructure information (PCII), was accessed or extracted.

Integrity and/or Confidentiality Loss

Sensitive or proprietary information was changed or deleted and/or Confidential information released to external parties.

 

Recoverability from the Incident: The size of the incident and impact will determine the amount of time and resources that must be spent on recovering from such incident.

 

Category

Definition

No effort

No recoverability effort needed

Regular

Time to recovery is predictable with existing resources

Supplemented

Time to recovery is predictable with additional resources

Extended

Time to recovery is unpredictable or even not possible, additional resources and outside help are required

 

Combining the functional impact to the Company’s systems and the impact to the Company’s information determines the business impact of the incident.

The recoverability determines the possible responses that the team may take when handling an incident. The team must prioritize the response to each incident based on its estimate of the business impact caused and the estimated efforts required to recover from it.

In Chapter 9, Appendix I, the Cybersecurity Incident Categorization Matrix combines the impact, recoverability, notification and further actions within an indicative timeframe.

17.20.4       Incident Response Plan

In case of cyber incidents on OT critical systems, notify the Company’s Emergency Report Team (ERT), in order for the Emergency Response Plan to get started.

 

Effective incident response is crucial during a cyber incident. The goal is to minimize impact and return systems to normal working order as soon as possible.

Responding to a cyber incident may however be beyond the competencies held within the Company and onboard the ships. In such cases, external expert assistance is required to ensure an effective response.

CYGNUS’s Emergency Incident Response should be triggered only when an event is associated with one of the aforementioned conditions in premises.

For maximum efficiency in Information Security Incident handling, specific escalation schemes should be followed.

In case of a potential incident, Security Operation Center should be immediately notified via phone call in order to escalate the event properly to Incident Responders. Maximum response time may vary based on the time and the impact of the incident.

Incident that can be handled remotely:

  • Working hours (09:00AM - 18:00PM) is set to five (5) minutes.
  • After office hours (18:00PM - 08:59AM) is set to fifteen (15) minutes.
  • Incident that needs physical access*.
  • Working hours (09:00AM - 18:00PM) is set to one (1) hour. After office hours (18:00PM - 08:59AM) is set to two (2) hours.

Incident Responders should have a user account ‘with administrative privileges, valid on every network asset. Administrative access is needed for investigation, containment and remediation phases. Account must be disabled and will only be enabled when an information security incident occurs.

There are 4 phases to an incident response:

Phase 1: Preparation

The Preparation phase covers the work the Company does to get ready for incident response, including establishing the right tools and resources and training the team.

To prepare for incidents:

  • Compile a list of IT/OT assets such as networks, servers and endpoints.
  • Employees and crew members should be trained in order to be able to identify simple security incidents based on company’s Training Procedures.
  • Identify their importance and which ones are critical or hold sensitive data.
  • Set up monitoring such as:
    • User activity
    • Network traffic
    • Installed software.
  • Determine which types of security events should be investigated.
  • Create detailed response steps for common types of incidents.

Phase 2: Detection and Analysis

Detection involves collecting data from IT/OT systems, security tools, publicly available information and people inside and outside the organization, and identifying precursors (signs that an incident may happen in the future) and indicators (data showing that an attack has happened or is happening now).

Analysis involves identifying a baseline of normal activity for the affected systems, correlating related events and seeing if and how they deviate from normal behavior.

Ascertain the following information:

  • How the incident occurred?
  • Which IT and/or OT systems were affected and how?
  • The extent to which the commercial and/or operational data is affected.
  • To what extend any threat to IT and OT systems remains?

Phase 3: Containment, Eradication and Recovery

Containing the outbreak of an incident is a time-critical exercise. The main goal of containment and eradication is the prompt limitation of the impact/damage and the prevention of any further damage to the same or other constituent systems. This includes the following steps:

  • Where possible, remove the system from the network. If it is not possible, then isolate the infected system from its network and ensure that boundary controls are operational between networks.
  • Check the firewall rules have not changed. Where systems are internet/VSAT facing, shut down remote access ports.
  • Ensure that anti-virus and anti-malware definitions are up to date.
  • Take a full disk/RAM image of any infected system for forensic investigation.

The purpose of recovery is to bring all affected systems back in normal operation.

IT, OT Systems and data are cleaned, recovered and restored to an operational condition. New PCs or equipment must be purchased if the incident is severe enough to necessitate this. Recovery plans for each system are covered in the next section.

Phase 4: Post Incident Activity

This phase helps to evaluate the reason of the incident outbreak, the missed precursors and new indications that must be added to the procedures for earlier detection and/or prevention:

  • Investigate the incident: To understand the causes and consequences of a cyber incident, the Company must undertake an investigation by completing the form NCR 003 “Incident Investigation Report” from Chapter 9 to report the cybersecurity incident. If the ship’s Flag has a specific form for cyber incident reporting, it must also be used supplementary. The information from the incident investigation is significant for preventing a potential reoccurrence.
  • Prevent re-occurrence: Taking into account the outcome of the investigation, actions to address any inadequacies in technical and/or procedural protection, measures are considered, in accordance with the Company procedures, for implementation of corrective actions.
  • Lessons Learnt: An essential part of following up a cyber security incident is to document, communicate and build on lessons learnt. This is an on-going process in order to learn from previous mistakes, incidents and experiences.

 

As such The Company for:

17.20.4.1     GDPR Data Breach Notification to Supervisory Authority

  • The company shall notify the supervisory authority without undue delay, of a personal data breach and where feasible not later than 72 hours.
  • Notification is made by email. Confirmation of receipt of this information is made by email.
  • The company assesses whether the personal data breach is likely to result in a risk to the rights and freedoms of the data subjects affected by the personal data breach.
  • The Company (data controller) shall provide the following information to the supervisory authority:
    • A description of the nature of the breach
    • The categories of personal data affected
    • Approximate number of data subjects affected
    • Approximate number of personal data records affected
    • Name and contact details of the person responsible for GDPR
    • Likely consequences of the breach
    • Any measures that have been or will be taken to address the breach, including mitigation.

 

Collection of evidence procedure:

All information gathered during the course of responding to an information security and personal data incident is potentially evidence to be used in a disciplinary, criminal or civil action.

IT Department is responsible for the collection and retention of information in respect of information security and personal data incidents.

  • Where the likelihood of legal, civil or criminal action is established early in the incident response process, the police or lawyers are involved as early as possible and their guidance is sought and followed in respect of evidence collection and retention.
  • External advisers or third parties are subject to NDA agreements.
  • In all other cases, all originals of paper documents have, attached to them, a statement describing precisely where, and under what conditions, it was found, who found it, who witnessed the event, together with a machine date-stamped photocopy of the document that indicates its original state.
  • Either:
    • The original computer media should be removed and retained securely
    • Copies of information on hard drives, in memory or on removable computer media should be taken (with a log of all actions during the copying process) with a witness present.
  • Paper documents or magnetic media must be kept securely.

17.20.4.2     Incident Response for Ships

Phase 1: Identification

Company’s ships crew members should be trained in order to be able to identify simple security incidents based on company’s Training Procedures. The ships crew immediately notifies the company’s IT department through phone.

Later on the Incident report from is completed and delivered to the company through e-mail.

Some possible scenarios for security incidents are:

  • You see a strange process running and accumulating a lot of CPU time.
  • Discovered an intruder logged into your system and changed files
  • Discovered a virus has infected your system. (through antivirus)
  • Determined that someone from a remote site is trying to penetrate the system.

=

Phase 2: Notification

Phase 3: Investigation & Security Incident Report

When an Information Security Incident is reported, the company’s IT Department will investigate the Information Security Incident in order to minimize the impact of the Information Security Incident on the affected system

IT department should review the received Incident Report Form from the ship and fill all the other fields that should be completed by the company containing the following. Date, time and place where the incident was found as well as detection conditions

  • Reporting ship
  • Dates and times of incident-related phone calls.
  • People you have contacted or have contacted you.
  • Other computer(s) onboard ship involved
  • Affected equipment(s)
  • Log from the system
  • Incident Type
    • Termination of service of unauthorized user.

Each incident report should be date, recording what happened, what was found and if other witnesses exist. Also, the normal functioning state (before the incident) must be ensured, to any extent possible.

Cyber Security drills are conducted on board on a six-month basis.

17.20.5       Incident Disaster Recovery (DR) Plan

The Company:

  • Defines the requirements for business continuity in the face of cyber threats.
  • Identifies risk conditions and plans against those risks so that business can continue even in case of serious interferences.
  • Plans and provides resources for disaster recovery to ensure business continuity or mission capabilities when responding to risk conditions.
  • Confirms that security architecture protecting its systems, facilities, personnel, and assets has adequate replication in terms of functions during a disaster recovery scenario.

Under no circumstance must a DR effort leave cybersecurity unmonitored.

 

Mission-critical functions are part of asset management. As such, the Company has plans in place to recover from these events. These plans might materialize by physical relocation, alternate equipment, alternative work regimes, or a combination of all.

Ashore & Onboard

  • Keep recovery plans for IT/OT servers, critical applications such as ECDIS and network equipment accessible to Officers onboard according to their responsibilities in the plans. The Officers and potential external IT personnel must understand this plan's purpose and scope.
  • Keep essential information and software backup facilities available to ensure recovery after a cyber incident.
  • Recovery of essential system functions related to the ship's safe operation may require ashore or third parties’ support assistance according to SLA’s services.
